title: Writing in 1st Grade: A Daily Routine
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: This Science of Reading Classroom post describes a daily writing routine called Power Up used by first grade teacher Stephane, introduced after her students had become comfortable connecting ideas. Students either stretch a kernel sentence or connect it to another idea using but or because, then finish with a three finger check for revision that covers reading it back, capitalization and punctuation. In the example lesson, students first discuss why Mercury has the shortest year, which retrieves earlier science learning, and then rehearse their sentence orally in pairs before writing. When one child forgets the kernel sentence, the teacher repeats his answer back, explains the error and lets him revise. The author likes the routine because it is simple enough for daily use, integrates oracy, writing and content, and holds young students to high standards of revision and editing.
points: Power Up has students either stretch a kernel sentence or connect it to another idea with but or because, which keeps the task focused and repeatable.
Discussing the content first, here why Mercury has the shortest year, both retrieves prior learning and prepares students to write well.
Oral rehearsal in pairs before writing supports the author's belief that oracy is the best rehearsal for writing.
The teacher responds to errors by repeating the student's answer, naming the mistake and allowing a revision.
A three finger check builds early habits of revision and editing even if children do not catch every error.
quotes: I like this routine for several reasons. First, it’s just really simple. You really can use it everyday.
Second, it seamlessly integrates oracy, writing, and content (and continues to reinforce my belief that oracy is the best rehearsal for writing).
Third, it holds students to high standards. It’s easy to skip revision in first grade, but this routine leans into it.
Even if kids aren’t going to catch every error they makes, it’s never too early to build habits around revision and editing.
Stephane explains that in this routine they will EITHER stretch a kernel sentence OR connect the kernel sentence to another idea using “but” or “because.
This discussion sets students up for success later on in their writing, AND it also gives the opportunity to retrieve and previously learned information about space and Mercury.
Finally, students check their sentences, using their three finger check (read aloud, capitalization, and punctuation) before chorally reading their complete sentence one last time.
